clue.text: Particular house, inside warm and snug

blocks.note: HO is the standard abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: An estate agent's line about a very specific cosy home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Particular' reads as an adjective describing the house, but it is the definition in its sense of fussy.
explanation.definitionFit: A particular person is fussy about what they accept, which is what choosy means.

clue.text: Spent LSD close to a Spanish region

indicators.note: spent letters are used up and scattered, so the fodder is broken and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Someone blows their old pounds, shillings and pence on a holiday near the Spanish coast.
explanation.walkthrough: LSD looks like old British money (pounds, shillings and pence) or the drug, but it is just three letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The Costa del Sol is the southern Spanish coastal region around Málaga.

clue.text: Better in bloom, ahead of function

blocks.note: flowers that are out are in bloom
a do is a party or social function

explanation.surface: A gardener says a plant is better once it flowers, ahead of some event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like an adjective, but it is the verb: to better someone is to outdo them.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to better a rival's effort is to surpass it.

clue.text: Establish colony around a US port

indicators.note: the settle word goes around the A

blocks.note: to settle a place is to establish a colony there

explanation.surface: Pioneers found a settlement near an American harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is historically apt: Seattle was itself founded by settlers.
explanation.definitionFit: Seattle is a major seaport in Washington State.

clue.text: Approaching fast in mini, men crashed by front of tavern

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: first letter of tavern, added to the fodder by 'by'

explanation.surface: Men in a Mini speed towards a pub and crash into its front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Approaching fast' reads as a car's speed but means soon to happen.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain adjective synonym for an event that is close at hand, as a storm or deadline draws near.

clue.text: Bureaucrat, and row about round fruit!

blocks.note: a mandarin is a senior civil servant
a range is a row, as of hills

explanation.surface: A civil servant argues over a round piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests a quarrel, but it is a line, a range.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this small, loose-skinned citrus is one kind of fruit.

clue.text: A metal may be extracted from it - there's iridium and gold in one

definitions.text: A metal may be extracted from it

blocks.note: Ir is the chemical symbol for iridium

explanation.surface: A mineral that yields a metal, containing both iridium and gold.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a descriptive phrase, fair because iron is the metal extracted.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the rock is mined and smelted to extract its metal.

clue.text: Girl given support from then on, till the end of time

definitions.text: from then on, till the end of time

blocks.note: a rafter is a supporting roof beam

explanation.surface: A girl is looked after from that moment until the end of time.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes the fairy-tale ending, happily ever after.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom, best known from fairy-tale endings, for continuing permanently from a given moment.

clue.text: Dostoyevsky's play?

indicators.note: the answer is the name's own, contained in its letters

blocks.note: three letters in the middle of the novelist's name, after the first three

explanation.walkthrough: The clue suggests a play written by Dostoyevsky, but he wrote novels; the answer sits inside his name.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to fiddle idly with something, as with food on a plate.

clue.text: Where juice may be obtained, satisfying Victoria in central London?

blocks.note: Victoria is a main-line railway station in central London

explanation.surface: Somewhere near Victoria in London that serves a satisfying glass of juice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Juice' is slang for fuel, so the juice bar picture is a decoy; a filling station is a petrol station.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang definition: juice is informal for petrol or fuel, which a forecourt sells.

clue.text: Funny series on radio? Poor audition cost me dearly, ultimately

indicators.note: a poor performance is badly put together, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A would-be comic regrets a bad audition for a radio comedy show.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: a sitcom can be on radio as well as television.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the full name of the sitcom, which often began life on radio before TV.

clue.text: I am no tall fizzy party drink

indicators.note: fizzy suggests bubbling agitation, so the letters are stirred up

explanation.surface: Someone declines a tall glass of fizz at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fizzy' seems to describe the drink, but amontillado is a still sherry; the word is only an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a medium-dry Spanish sherry is one kind of drink.

clue.text: Section of curve in semicircular channel

indicators.note: the answer is found in the words that follow

blocks.note: the last two letters of semicircular plus the first of channel

explanation.surface: An anatomy note on the curved canals of the inner ear.
explanation.walkthrough: Semicircular canals are in the inner ear, so the anatomy picture hides a plain geometry answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A geometric term: any continuous part of a curve, such as part of a circle.

clue.text: Cultivated, hence taller mushroom

indicators.note: cultivated ground is turned over, so the letters are dug up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A farmed mushroom grows taller than a wild one.
explanation.walkthrough: Chanterelles are in fact wild and hard to cultivate, so 'Cultivated' is purely the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a funnel-shaped, apricot-scented yellow fungus prized by cooks.

clue.text: Old record with new inset showing pop group's manager

indicators.note: a new version of the word is a rearranged one

blocks.note: an EP (extended play) is an old record format

explanation.surface: An old record with a new sleeve insert shows the band's manager.
explanation.walkthrough: Brian Epstein managed the Beatles, so the pop-group definition is a specific person.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Brian, who managed the Beatles, the pop group of pop groups.

clue.text: Being clearer about New England, one may make a point

blocks.note: NE is the standard abbreviation for New England

explanation.surface: Someone being clearer about New England makes a point in an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make a point' reads as arguing, but it is literal: a pencil sharpener makes a point.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the tool literally puts a point on a pencil or knife.

clue.text: A disinclination to act in opening of Educating Rita, possibly

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An actor is reluctant to perform in the opening of the play Educating Rita.
explanation.walkthrough: Educating Rita, a Willy Russell play and film, is split apart: only its first letter and the name Rita are used.
explanation.definitionFit: The figurative sense of a physics term: sluggish reluctance to move or change.

clue.text: Spots, while talking, a town on the Thames

indicators.note: while talking means we hear the word, not read it

explanation.surface: Someone notices marks on their clothes while chatting in a riverside town.
explanation.walkthrough: Staines (now Staines-upon-Thames) is a town west of London, in Surrey.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a Surrey commuter town west of London, officially renamed upon-Thames in 2012.

clue.text: Still in ignorance, at the present time, over planned rise

indicators.note: planned letters are arranged to a new design

explanation.surface: An employee still does not know about the pay rise that was planned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Planned rise' reads as a pay rise, but planned is the anagram signal and rise the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for having learnt nothing, as in coming away none the better informed.

clue.text: Working with improved remit, deservedly so

indicators.note: an improved version has been reworked, its letters rearranged

blocks.note: a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Someone given a better job description has earned it.
explanation.walkthrough: A remit is one's area of responsibility at work, so the office picture is complete.
explanation.definitionFit: Something won on merit is deservedly won.

clue.text: Examination claimed to be fixed

indicators.note: the letters need fixing, put into a different order

explanation.surface: Someone alleges an exam was rigged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Examination' suggests a school test, but it is the noun medical, a check-up.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective used as a noun: a doctor's check-up, as for a job or insurance.

clue.text: Circuit friend recalled

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the word runs back

explanation.surface: A friend from the racing circuit is remembered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalled' suggests memory, but here it turns the friend word round.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from racing: one complete trip round the track.

clue.text: Gradual damage caused by Durham river trade, staggering article covered

indicators.note: staggering letters lurch out of order

blocks.note: the Wear flows through Durham in north-east England
anagram fodder, with the article inside

explanation.surface: A river's commerce in Durham is being slowly worn down.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wear is the river running through the city of Durham; the article inside the trade letters is then mixed in.
explanation.definitionFit: Wear and tear is damage that builds up gradually through use.

clue.text: Call up? That's all right during the night before a festival

blocks.note: an eve is the night before a festival, as Christmas Eve

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a phone call is fine on the night before a festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call up' reads as phoning, but it means summoning up a memory or feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to summon a memory or feeling into the mind.

clue.text: Come out? Some who went here may have done so afterwards

definitions.text: Come out? Some who went here may have done so afterwards

blocks.note: the surface reads 'leave' or 'emerge'; really it is a debutante's coming out into society

blocks.clueFragment: Some who went here may have done so afterwards
blocks.note: reads like leaving a building; really pupils made their debut after finishing their schooling

explanation.walkthrough: 'Come out' is the debutante's debut in society, which girls from a finishing school might make after leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: A finishing school prepared young women for society, where debutantes came out.

clue.text: Francs alumnus got out of pocket

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for francs
OB = old boy, a former pupil

explanation.surface: A former pupil loses francs, out of pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of pocket' is a decoy phrase: pocket alone is the definition, a fob being a small watch pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: A fob is a small pocket in a waistcoat or trousers for a watch.

clue.text: Russell, perhaps - Russell, perhaps squeezing 'er tight, initially

explanation.surface: One Russell hugs a woman tightly.
explanation.walkthrough: The same phrase appears twice: first it is the philosopher Bertrand Russell, then the comedian Russell Brand.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertrand Russell was the philosopher, so Bertrand is an example of a Russell's first name.

clue.text: Charge exorbitantly for wool

blocks.note: a verb here: to swindle a customer with a steep price

explanation.walkthrough: A sheep's fleece is its wool, and to fleece someone is to overcharge them, so the two senses meet in the idea of shearing.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece is to overcharge; a fleece is a sheep's coat of wool.
